Acknowledged technical limitations severely limit applicability: method overgeneralizes details on high-degradation inputs, fails to fully remove degradation in some cases, shares failure modes with existing approaches
Misleading scope framing: claims 'Video Restoration' but experiments narrowly focus on 4× upscaling only; no exploration of diverse degradations or restoration tasks
Prohibitive reproducibility barriers: requires 72 H100-80G GPUs for training; no code available; many hyperparameter choices lack justification
Insufficient analysis: no theoretical justification for adaptive window mechanism; missing visualization of learned representations; minimal failure case characterization

All experiments confined to single 4× upscaling scenario; generalization to other scales, degradations, or restoration tasks unexplored

strengths: Clear practical contribution with strong empirical results: achieves comparable quality to multi-step diffusion methods at 4× speedup, demonstrating genuine practical value for real-world video restoration applications

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple diverse datasets (synthetic and real-world) with both quantitative metrics and qualitative comparisons, supported by ablation studies and user studies
Well-engineered technical approach that effectively combines existing techniques (Swin-MMDIT, APT) with meaningful improvements including adaptive window attention and progressive distillation
Excellent presentation with clear methodology figures, sufficient implementation details for reproducibility, and thoughtful discussion of limitations and societal impacts
Solid ablation studies (Table 3) that convincingly demonstrate the contribution of each component, showing proper scientific rigor in validating design choices
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily an engineering contribution combining existing techniques rather than introducing fundamentally new ideas; adaptive window attention is a straightforward solution to a known problem
Insufficient justification for key design choices: feature matching loss (Eq. 4) lacks theoretical motivation, and selection of which discriminator blocks to use appears arbitrary without ablation

Acknowledged robustness limitations: method fails on very heavy degradations, exhibits overgeneralization on high-degradation inputs, and struggles with large motions, limiting practical deployment scenarios

Incomplete analysis of hyperparameter sensitivity: loss weights appear somewhat arbitrary with limited ablation on sensitivity to weight selection, R2 regularization, and other critical hyperparameters
Missing computational cost analysis: training requires 72 H100 GPUs but lacks detailed discussion of training efficiency, cost comparison with baselines, or computational scaling analysis
User study limitations: only 25 samples evaluated with no inter-rater agreement metrics, statistical significance testing, or comprehensive human evaluation protocol details

Progressive distillation justification lacks depth: the strategy is presented as a solution to training instability but without clear formalization of why this particular schedule was chosen or theoretical grounding

Limited novelty in individual components: RpGAN and R2 regularization are incremental adaptations of existing techniques; the overall contribution is engineering-focused rather than introducing novel concepts

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets and metrics with extensive baseline comparisons
Clear problem motivation and well-articulated need for efficient one-step diffusion-based video restoration
Technically sound execution with reasonable engineering choices and implementation details
Extensive ablation studies (Table 3) examining training components and adaptive window attention mechanism
Good visual results demonstrating competitive performance on restoration tasks with fine detail preservation
Reproducibility commitment including implementation details and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty - core contributions (adaptive window attention, feature matching loss, progressive distillation) are straightforward extensions or combinations of existing techniques without clear innovation
Misleading speedup claims: '4x faster' comparison is against multi-step methods rather than other one-step approaches; inherent speedup of one-step sampling is not a methodological contribution
Weak experimental validation: user study (Table 2) shows only marginal improvements over baselines (often <5%), contradicting main claims of superiority

Unfair comparison with concurrent work: DOVE (Chen et al., 2025b) discovered similar ideas independently but only brief appendix discussion; no direct quantitative comparison despite being critical for novelty assessment

Ad-hoc design choices lacking justification: loss function weighting (all 1.0 without ablation), discriminator block selection (16th, 26th, 36th) appears arbitrary, feature matching loss design not motivated

Significant acknowledged limitations inadequately addressed: failures on 720p videos with 100 frames, poor performance on heavy degradations and AIGC videos, no proposed solutions or failure mode analysis
Real-world performance gaps: results on VideoLQ (real data) substantially weaker than synthetic benchmarks, raising generalization concerns
Experimental evaluation issues: small user study sample (25 samples), heavy reliance on metrics with known failure modes, mixing of synthetic/real datasets, unclear methodology for 'technical score'
Reproducibility barriers despite promises: requires 72 NVIDIA H100-80G GPUs for one day training, initialization dependency on SeedVR model, many hyperparameters not clearly specified
Presentation clarity: dense writing with scattered design choices, Figure 2 cluttered and difficult to parse, main contributions not clearly separated from technical details

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical value: one-step diffusion-based video restoration is challenging and underexplored, with significant computational efficiency gains demonstrated

Solid technical contributions: adaptive window attention elegantly handles arbitrary resolution inputs; feature matching loss addresses real computational bottlenecks; progressive distillation and RpGAN loss improve training stability

Comprehensive experimental validation: extensive baseline comparisons, evaluation on multiple synthetic and real-world datasets, multiple evaluation metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, NIQE, MUSIQ, DOVR, VMAF, CLIP-IQA), user study validation, and systematic ablation studies

Strong empirical results: achieves comparable/superior quality to multi-step methods with approximately 4x speedup, scales to high-resolution videos, and shows impressive visual quality with fine detail preservation
Excellent presentation: clear writing, well-motivated sections, outstanding visualizations of results and comparisons, comprehensive supplementary materials
Good reproducibility efforts: implementation details provided, ethics statement included, comprehensive ablation studies, and promise of code release
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual components: adaptive window mechanisms exist in vision transformers, APT is from prior work (Lin et al., 2025), and progressive distillation/feature matching are relatively straightforward; main novelty is in their combination rather than fundamental innovation

Insufficient theoretical justification: why does feature matching outperform LPIPS for this task beyond empirical validation? Why is adaptive attention specifically necessary versus existing methods? Design choices like 3×3 partition lack explicit justification

Acknowledged but unresolved robustness limitations: not robust to heavy degradations, over-generates details on 720p AIGC videos, and VAE efficiency bottleneck (4x slower than image VAE) are significant practical limitations

Reproducibility barriers: code/models only promised 'upon acceptance' (not available for review), requires 72 NVIDIA H100-80GB GPUs for training, and 8.2B parameter model size limit practical adoption

Limited evaluation scope: primarily focuses on common degradations (blur, noise, compression) with limited evaluation on other degradation types (rain, snow) or domains; 4K evaluation claimed in abstract but limited in practice

Insufficient comparison with concurrent work: DOVE (Chen et al., 2025b) is contemporary but comparisons relegated to appendix; key differences and relative advantages not clearly articulated in main paper
Limited user study: only 25 samples with simple GSB metric provides relatively weak perceptual validation; MGLD-VSR still outperforms on RED530, contradicting claimed superiority
Insufficient analysis of design choices: missing failure case analysis, limited cross-dataset generalization study, no analysis of which loss components contribute most to performance
